claims.text: Big-O describes how the work of a piece of code grows with the input size, keeping only the fastest-growing part of the cost and ignoring constant factors.
claims.source_hint: csharp/fundamentals/statements/collections.md l.53 TIP (meaning of O(1) and O(n) as growth with collection size)

claims.text: One lookup by key in a Dictionary<TKey,TValue> costs about the same however many entries the dictionary holds.
claims.source_hint: standard/collections/index.md l.77 complexity table (Dictionary<T> lookup O(1) amortized); Dictionary<TKey,TValue> API remarks: retrieval is O(1)

claims.text: When each step discards half of the items still under consideration, the number of steps grows by one each time the input size doubles; that growth is written O(log n).
claims.source_hint: definition of the base-2 logarithm: halving n repeatedly reaches 1 in log2(n) steps

claims.text: A loop over one collection placed inside a loop over another costs the product of the two sizes, not their sum; over the same collection of n items that is n × n, written O(n²).
claims.source_hint: arithmetic of nested iteration; csharp/fundamentals/statements/collections.md l.53 TIP for the O() notation

claims.text: 12 orders against 5 customers cost 60 comparisons in a loop inside a loop; 1,000 against 1,000 cost 1,000,000.
claims.source_hint: arithmetic: 12 × 5 = 60, 1000 × 1000 = 1000000; the second number is printed by NestedLoops.Run at stage-0

claims.text: Putting a collection in order with the sort the .NET library gives you costs O(n log n) (List<T>.Sort, Array.Sort, OrderBy); it sits between linear and quadratic on the ladder O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²).
claims.source_hint: List<T>.Sort API remarks, net-10.0 ("This method is an O(n log n) operation, where n is Count"); core/compatibility/core-libraries/5.0/orderby-firstordefault-complexity-increase.md l.14

claims.text: Because Big-O drops constant factors, two passes over a collection and one pass over it are both O(n), and a quadratic method with a cheap body can run faster than a linear one with an expensive body while n stays small.
claims.source_hint: csharp/fundamentals/statements/collections.md l.53 TIP (O() ignores constants); standard texts on asymptotic notation

claims.text: Read the shape off the loops and off any call that itself walks or searches a collection, not off the number of statements; estimate first, then measure, because the estimate is cheap enough to do while reading the code while only a measurement settles what the constants do at the size you run at.
In the example repository at tag stage-0, DonHang.Samples is a console project whose runner registers this sample under the name nested-loops, and NestedLoops.Run builds two arrays of 1,000 ids.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang at stage-0: samples/DonHang.Samples/Program.cs l.19; Samples/Data/NestedLoops.cs l.29-30

claims.text: new HashSet<int>(customerIds) copies the elements of the given collection into the set in a single pass over it.
claims.source_hint: System.Collections.Generic.HashSet<T>(IEnumerable<T>) constructor remarks: this operation is O(n), where n is the number of elements in the collection

claims.text: Enumerable.Count with a predicate walks the source sequence once, applying the predicate to each element; HashSet<T>.Contains answers by hash code, so each lookup costs about the same whatever the set holds, as long as the hash codes spread the items out.
claims.source_hint: fundamentals/code-analysis/quality-rules/ca1851.md l.93 (a LINQ count enumerates the sequence); standard/collections/index.md l.77, l.84 (HashSet<T> lookup O(1) amortized, O(n) worst case)

claims.text: Without an index PostgreSQL answers a WHERE by reading every row of the table, so the work grows in step with the number of rows.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs ch. 11.1 Introduction to Indexes ("the system would have to scan the entire test1 table, row by row")

claims.text: Big-O does not predict a duration: it drops the constants that machine speed and per-item cost are made of, so the same shape takes different times on different machines and different data.
claims.source_hint: csharp/fundamentals/statements/collections.md l.53 TIP (O() describes growth, not elapsed time)

claims.text: An inner loop over a collection whose size does not grow with the input multiplies the cost by a constant, leaving the overall shape linear rather than quadratic.
claims.source_hint: arithmetic of nested iteration with a fixed inner bound k: n × k is a constant multiple of n

claims.text: O(1) means the cost does not change as the input grows; it says nothing about how large that unchanging cost is, so a constant-time step can be slower than many cheap comparisons.
claims.source_hint: csharp/fundamentals/statements/collections.md l.53 TIP (O(1) defined as independent of collection size, not as 'fast')

claims.text: Running `dotnet run --project samples/DonHang.Samples -- nested-loops` at tag stage-0 prints `slow way: 1000 matches, 1000000 comparisons` and then `fast way: 1000 matches, 1000 lookups`.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang at stage-0: samples/DonHang.Samples/Samples/Data/NestedLoops.cs l.27-34 — run it

claims.text: With both arrays at 2,000 ids the quadratic count makes 4,000,000 comparisons and the linear one makes 2,000 lookups: doubling the input doubles the linear cost and quadruples the quadratic one.
The two operation counts the sample prints (1000000 comparisons, 1000 lookups) are literal text in NestedLoops.Run, worked out from the shapes; neither method counts its own operations.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang at stage-0: samples/DonHang.Samples/Samples/Data/NestedLoops.cs l.32-33 — the counts are inside the format strings, not computed
